blocks.text: The goal of this station is to demonstrate that you understand how suction apparatus removes secretions, blood, vomitus, and other fluids from the airway or a body cavity. You must be able to identify its components, assemble it, demonstrate safe operation, recognize complications, and explain its use in adults, children, and neonates.
Name: Suction apparatus (suction machine or aspirator).
Classification: A therapeutic and emergency medical device that uses negative pressure to aspirate fluids and secretions.
Principle of operation: The machine generates negative pressure (vacuum), creating a pressure difference that draws fluid through a suction catheter or tubing into a collection container.
1. Portable electric suction machine
Used in emergency departments, ambulances, wards, clinics, and home care. It operates using mains electricity, a rechargeable battery, or both.
2. Wall-mounted suction
Connected to a central hospital vacuum supply. The regulator controls the suction pressure, while the collection canister traps aspirated fluids.
3. Manual suction device
Operated by hand or foot. Useful in selected settings where electrical power is unavailable, provided the device is appropriate for the intended patient and clinical task.
Examiner's expected answer:

"This is a suction apparatus. It is used to remove secretions, blood, vomitus, and other fluids by applying controlled negative pressure. It is commonly used for airway clearance and for suctioning fluids during certain clinical procedures."

rows: Airway obstruction by secretions
Clears the airway when the patient cannot clear secretions independently.
Unconscious patient
Removes accessible oral secretions or vomitus when indicated.
Tracheostomy or endotracheal tube
Removes retained secretions from the artificial airway.
Neonatal resuscitation
Selective suction when secretions obstruct breathing or interfere with ventilation.
Surgical procedures
Removes blood and fluids from the operative field.
Oral and dental procedures
Removes saliva, blood, and irrigation fluids.
Drainage of selected body cavities
Aspirates fluids when required by a specific procedure.

blocks.text: Important distinction: Suction apparatus is not automatically indicated whenever secretions are present. Routine suctioning can cause trauma, hypoxia, bradycardia, and other complications. Suction only when clinically indicated and according to the relevant protocol.
A. Vacuum pump or vacuum source
Generates negative pressure. In wall suction, the vacuum source is the hospital's central system.
B. Pressure regulator and gauge
The regulator adjusts the suction level; the gauge indicates the vacuum pressure, commonly in mmHg or kPa.
C. Collection canister
Collects aspirated fluids and allows approximate measurement of the collected volume.
D. Connecting tubing
Transfers the negative pressure and aspirated material between the collection canister and catheter.
E. Suction catheter or Yankauer tip
The catheter enters the airway when indicated; a Yankauer is a relatively rigid oral suction tip used to remove accessible oral secretions.
F. Bacterial filter and overflow protection
Depending on the model, these help prevent fluid or contamination from entering the pump and protect the equipment.
Other possible components include an on/off switch, battery indicator, foot pedal, catheter connector, and a pressure-release control.
Exam tip: Be able to point to the pressure regulator, gauge, collection canister, tubing, and suction tip on the actual apparatus.

items.text: Rapid removal of secretions and fluids.
Can help restore airway patency when obstruction is caused by accessible secretions.
Portable models allow use during transport and emergencies.
Adjustable suction pressure permits appropriate settings for different patients and procedures.
Collection canisters allow approximate assessment of aspirated volume and appearance.
Compatible with a range of suction tips and catheters.
Excessive negative pressure can injure mucosa and cause bleeding.
Airway suction can cause hypoxaemia and vagally mediated bradycardia.
It may provoke coughing, discomfort, laryngospasm, or bronchospasm.
Thick secretions may obstruct the catheter.
It cannot correct airway obstruction caused by a foreign body that cannot be safely removed through suction.
It does not replace oxygenation, ventilation, or definitive airway management.
Portable machines depend on adequate battery charge or another available power source.
Inadequate cleaning, incorrect assembly, or a full canister can compromise function and infection control.

blocks.text: Before using the device, explain the procedure where possible, assess the patient, and use appropriate personal protective equipment.
Equipment checklist

items.text: Confirm the machine is functional and the power supply or battery is adequate.
Check the collection canister, lid, tubing, and connections.
Ensure the overflow shut-off and protective filter are correctly fitted if present.
Select an appropriate suction tip or catheter size.
Confirm the catheter is sterile when sterile airway suction is required.
Check the pressure gauge and set an appropriate pressure.
Test suction by briefly occluding the tubing or using the manufacturer's recommended test method.
Ensure oxygen, monitoring, and resuscitation equipment are available when clinically indicated.

blocks.text: Patient preparation

items.text: Explain the procedure and obtain consent where feasible.
Assess respiratory rate, work of breathing, oxygen saturation, heart rate, and level of consciousness as appropriate.
Position the patient to facilitate safe suctioning.
Provide pre-oxygenation when indicated, especially for patients at risk of desaturation.
Use appropriate hand hygiene, gloves, and eye or face protection when splashing is possible.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. How to use it: Step-by-step OSCE demonstration

blocks.text: Introduce and assess
"I would introduce myself, confirm the patient's identity, explain the procedure, assess the indication for suction, and obtain consent where possible."
Prepare the equipment
Perform hand hygiene, put on appropriate PPE, inspect the apparatus, connect the tubing and collection canister, and attach the appropriate suction tip or catheter.
Set and test the pressure
Switch on the machine, occlude the tubing briefly according to the manufacturer's instructions, and adjust the regulator to the prescribed level. Do not begin with unnecessarily high suction.
Position the patient
Position appropriately for the clinical situation. Ensure the airway can be accessed safely and that oxygenation and monitoring are available when required.
Perform suction

For oral suction, use a suitable Yankauer tip and remove visible secretions carefully. For tracheal or endotracheal suction, use the appropriate catheter and the relevant airway-specific protocol. Apply suction during withdrawal, not during insertion, for conventional open tracheal suction.
Monitor the patient

Observe oxygen saturation, heart rate, respiratory effort, colour, and response throughout. Keep each suction pass brief; for adult tracheal suction, it is generally limited to no more than 15 seconds, with shorter passes often appropriate for children and neonates.
Reassess and document

Allow recovery between passes, provide oxygenation support as indicated, and reassess whether further suction is necessary. Document the indication, secretions, patient response, and any complications.
Finish safely
Dispose of single-use items correctly, clean or replace reusable components according to infection-control policy, and ensure the apparatus is ready for its next use.
Critical OSCE point: Do not routinely instil normal saline into an endotracheal tube before suctioning. It is not recommended as a routine practice.
There are few absolute contraindications to clinically necessary suction, but the procedure should be justified and performed cautiously.

items.text: Recent airway surgery or trauma.
Significant bleeding tendency or friable airway mucosa.
Severe hypoxaemia or haemodynamic instability.
Suspected raised intracranial pressure, where coughing or physiological disturbance may be harmful.
Airway abnormalities that increase the risk of trauma.

blocks.text: These circumstances require individual assessment; necessary lifesaving suction should not be withheld solely because a relative risk is present.

rows: Hypoxaemia
Limit suction duration, monitor oxygenation, and provide oxygenation support as indicated.
Bradycardia
Avoid prolonged or excessive suction; stop if significant bradycardia develops and manage the patient urgently.
Mucosal trauma and bleeding
Use an appropriate catheter, pressure, and technique.
Laryngospasm or bronchospasm
Use gentle technique; stop and manage if these occur.
Infection
Maintain hand hygiene, aseptic technique, and proper equipment processing.
Atelectasis
Avoid excessive negative pressure and unnecessarily prolonged suction.
Raised intracranial pressure
Minimise stimulation and monitor high-risk patients appropriately.

blocks.text: The suction machine itself does not generate a diagnostic test result in the usual sense. However, you should assess the aspirated material and the patient's response.

rows: Small amounts of clear or whitish secretions
May be normal, depending on the patient and clinical context.
Thick, tenacious secretions
May occur with dehydration or impaired secretion clearance.
Yellow or green secretions
May occur with airway inflammation or infection; colour alone does not establish a bacterial infection.
Fresh blood
May indicate mucosal trauma, airway bleeding, or another pathology.
Pink, frothy secretions
Can occur with pulmonary oedema in the appropriate clinical context.
No secretions obtained
May mean suction is unnecessary, the catheter is misplaced or blocked, or the system is malfunctioning.

blocks.text: Also assess whether breathing, air entry, oxygen saturation, and visible airway obstruction improve after suction.
Pediatric suctioning requires particular attention because infants and children have smaller airways and can deteriorate rapidly.

items.text: Catheter size: Select according to the child's airway and the internal diameter of any artificial airway. An oversized catheter can obstruct airflow and cause trauma.
Pressure: Use age-appropriate, protocol-based suction pressure rather than adult settings.
Duration: Use the shortest effective pass. Neonatal and pediatric suction passes are commonly shorter than adult passes.
Monitoring: Observe heart rate and oxygen saturation, particularly in neonates and critically ill children.
Technique: Avoid unnecessary deep suctioning; suction only as far as indicated by the procedure and airway protocol.
Oxygenation: Consider pre-oxygenation where indicated, balancing the risk of hypoxaemia against the risks of excessive oxygen, particularly in preterm infants.

Neonatal resuscitation: Routine suctioning is not recommended simply because a newborn is delivered through meconium-stained fluid. Prioritise effective ventilation when indicated; suction is reserved for suspected airway obstruction or specific clinical indications.

blocks.text: Examiner's question: Why are neonates particularly vulnerable to suction complications?

Model answer: Their small airways are easily obstructed by a catheter, their oxygen reserve is limited, and suction-induced hypoxaemia or vagal stimulation can rapidly cause bradycardia and deterioration.
Select
Select the appropriate catheter and suction pressure.
Understand
Understand the indication and explain the procedure.
Check
Check the machine, tubing, canister, and filter.
Technique
Use the correct technique and maintain infection control.
Inspect
Inspect secretions and monitor the patient's response.
Observe
Observe oxygenation, heart rate, and respiratory effort.
Note
Note the findings, document, and clean the equipment.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Common OSCE questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the principle of suction apparatus?
It creates negative pressure, drawing secretions or fluids through a catheter or suction tip into a collection canister.
Q2. What is the difference between a Yankauer tip and a suction catheter?

A Yankauer is a relatively rigid tip mainly used for oral suction. A flexible suction catheter is used for more specific applications, including tracheal suction through an artificial airway when indicated.
Q3. Why is the collection canister necessary?
It collects aspirated fluids, prevents contamination of the vacuum source when used with appropriate protection, and permits approximate measurement of the aspirate.
Q4. What should you do if the machine is switched on but suction is inadequate?

Check the power supply, regulator setting, tubing connections, leaks, catheter blockage, canister seal, and filter or overflow protection. Use an alternative functioning device if urgent suction is needed.
Q5. What should you do if the patient develops bradycardia during suction?

Stop suction immediately, withdraw the catheter, support oxygenation and ventilation as necessary, and assess the patient. Initiate the appropriate emergency response if bradycardia persists or the patient deteriorates.
Q6. Why should suction pressure not be excessively high?
Excessive negative pressure increases the risk of mucosal injury, bleeding, hypoxaemia, atelectasis, and other complications.
Q7. When should you suction a newborn's airway?
When secretions are obstructing the airway or interfering with effective ventilation, rather than routinely suctioning every newborn.
Q8. What is the difference between open and closed suction?

items.text: Open suction: The ventilator circuit may need to be disconnected, and a sterile single-use catheter is passed into the artificial airway.
Closed suction: A catheter enclosed in a protective sleeve is used without disconnecting the ventilator circuit, helping maintain ventilation and PEEP.

blocks.text: Q9. What is the purpose of the pressure gauge?
It indicates the negative pressure generated by the system, helping the operator set and verify an appropriate suction level.
Q10. Is suction apparatus used only for airway clearance?
No. It is also used to remove fluids during surgical, dental, and selected drainage procedures.
Mistake: Applying maximum suction pressure
Correction: Select the appropriate pressure for the patient, device, and procedure.
Mistake: Suctioning continuously or for too long
Correction: Use brief, controlled passes and reassess between them.
Mistake: Forgetting monitoring
Correction: Monitor the patient's clinical state and oxygenation throughout when indicated.
Mistake: Ignoring the overflow protection
Correction: Check that the canister is not full and that protective components are fitted correctly.
What impresses the examiner
State the indication, check the equipment, demonstrate safe assembly, explain pressure control, monitor the patient, and describe what you would do if complications occur.
